attribution: US Army Air Corps / National Archives (NARA 23935539)
depicts: An Army Air Corps record photograph of the Golden Gate Bridge District's public progress billboard, standing in scrub grass beside a dirt road with a white lattice skirt beneath it and a plain wooden fence in front. The board carries a painted elevation of the finished bridge with a row of thermometer-style gauges marking percentage completion of each contract; a car and two shed roofs are just visible behind it at left and right.
details: No people. The board reads THE GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE across the top and 'A $35,000,000 PROJECT / STARTED 1933 / COMPLETION 1937' across the middle, with 'Joseph B. Strauss, Chief Engineer' under the span. The lower band lists every contractor by work package — McClintic-Marshall Corp. (main steel structures), John A. Roebling's Sons (main cables), Pacific Bridge Co. (main piers and fender), Barrett & Hilp (anchorages), Eaton and Smith, Alta Electric — and, at right, the full Bridge District directorate by name and county. The individual completion thermometers stand at wildly different heights; the master gauge in the centre is under half full. This is the direct visual for the $35 million figure that the era's 'one death per million dollars' rule of thumb was applied to.
visible_text: Typed at top: 'Rec'd from Crissy Field, Calif. - 5/13/35' and 'Golden Gate Bridge - San Francisco, Calif. to Marin County, Calif.'. Burned into lower left of print: '(G52-32I-15)(4-5-35-11:00A.) GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE DATA.' Board text: 'THE GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE', 'A $35,000,000 PROJECT', 'TOTAL LENGTH 6450 FEET', 'THE TOTAL PROJECT PROGRESS SCHEDULE — Percentage Completed Mar 1st 1935 is shown in red', 'CONTRACTORS', 'Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District Directorate'. Stamped 'INDEXED' at bottom.
notes: Dated 5 April 1935 on the print, received at Crissy Field 13 May 1935. Photographed as a flat copy of the sign, so it reads as a document rather than a landscape. Useful for wages/cost/contractor material rather than for men.

license: No known copyright restrictions (Internet Archive Book Images, from Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933)
attribution: Architect and Engineer / San Francisco Public Library, via Internet Archive Book Images
depicts: A halftone magazine plate. Four men stand in a loose line on bare graded ground at the left foreground, in front of the enormous blank concrete face of a bridge anchorage block that fills the right two-thirds of the frame. Five more small figures stand on top of the anchorage against the sky, one of them beside what looks like a surveyor's tripod. A timber ladder and a dark tarpaulin hang down the far left edge of the concrete.
details: Nine men total. The four in the foreground are hatless — no hard hats at all, this being 1933, three years before Strauss's hard-hat rule was in force. Two wear ordinary business suits and street shoes; one wears a suit with a soft hat held in his hand; the third from left is dressed for the site in a work jacket, jodhpur-cut breeches and tall laced field boots. Nobody is tied off; the five men on the anchorage roof stand casually at the unguarded edge with a drop of several storeys behind them. The scale contrast — men the height of one concrete lift — is the point of the picture. No safety net (deck construction is years away).
visible_text: Printed caption at bottom left: '"Golden Gate" Cement used.'
notes: From the trade journal Architect and Engineer, 1933, digitised by San Francisco Public Library. The men are almost certainly engineers, inspectors and cement-company representatives rather than the ironworker gangs, which is worth saying if narration points at them. One of only two 1930s Golden Gate site photographs in this pool with clearly readable people.

attribution: US National Park Service — Golden Gate NRA, Park Archives, Muir Woods Collection, GOGA 32470.1736
depicts: A group portrait of the Muir Woods Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Fort Baker, taken on a dirt road with the Golden Gate Bridge under construction rising behind them. Roughly sixty young men in dark work clothes are packed into and around a line of six Model A-era open trucks and cars parked nose-out across the frame; two older men in a suit and in riding breeches stand apart at the far left beside a sedan. Behind and above them the raw concrete Marin anchorage block sits on a bare cut hillside, with the steel north tower still only part-built at the far left and a lattice radio mast in the middle distance.
details: About sixty men and boys, nearly all bare-headed, a handful in flat caps and a few in light-coloured campaign hats; several are standing on running boards and truck beds to get into frame, some grinning, one waving. They are CCC enrollees — Depression relief labour — not bridge workers, but the picture puts a Depression-era workforce of young men in the same frame as the half-built bridge. No hard hats, no safety equipment of any kind. Construction shacks, a generator trailer, spoil heaps and a sign reading '...OP / ...NT' are scattered on the left. The Marin anchorage is still unformed concrete with timber falsework crowning it.
visible_text: Printed along the bottom margin: 'Golden Gate NRA, Park Archives, Muir Woods Collection, GOGA 32470.1736'
notes: Only 1024px on the long edge — usable full-frame but will not stand a hard push-in. The best single image in this pool for the Depression / 25% unemployment / relief-labour context.

license: No known copyright restrictions (Flickr Commons). SFPL note: commercial use requires permission from the San Francisco History Center.
attribution: San Francisco News-Call Bulletin Photo Morgue, San Francisco History Center, San Francisco Public Library
depicts: A man in a hard hat stands on a bare timber working platform at the very top of a Golden Gate Bridge tower, playing a trombone out over the strait. The Marin Headlands and the water of the Golden Gate fall away hundreds of feet below and behind him. A riveted steel strut and a derrick boom cut diagonally across the left of the frame; wooden rivet kegs, a coiled length of hose, a steel drum and a scatter of tools lie on the planking to his right.
details: Three men. The trombonist is the subject: dark round hard hat with a curled cord hanging from it, leather jacket, dark trousers, two-tone street shoes, standing squarely on the edge of the plank deck with no rail, no harness and nothing between him and the water. Down at lower left two more workers on the steel below him — one in a light-coloured hard hat, one bare-headed — are working with their backs to the camera. Four wooden rivet kegs and a fifth barrel sit at right; loose steel bars, a sledge and a length of chain are strewn across the boards. No safety net is visible: at this height, above the deck line, there was none. The casualness of a man playing a horn on that plank is the whole picture.
notes: SFPL identifies the man as Jess Stafford, a San Francisco bandleader, posed for a newspaper stunt photo c. 1936 — so he is a publicity subject rather than an ironworker, and narration should not call him a worker. The hard hat, the platform, the tools and the two genuine workers behind him are all real. Portrait orientation. The single strongest 'men on high steel' image found at usable resolution.

license: No known copyright restrictions (Flickr Commons). SFPL note: commercial use requires permission from the San Francisco History Center.
attribution: San Francisco History Center, San Francisco Public Library
depicts: Looking up at the underside of the catwalk during erection. A steep diagonal ladder-like catwalk runs from lower right up to a timber working platform at upper left, cantilevered out into blank white sky over the strait, with the Marin hills as a pale ridge along the right. Guy wires and cables slice across the frame. Men are strung out along the catwalk and clustered on the platform.
details: Eight men visible. Five are grouped on the timber platform at upper left, standing and crouching around what appear to be tools and a coil of line; one of them wears a light-coloured hat, the others darker caps or hard hats. One man is walking up the open catwalk in the middle of the frame with nothing on either side of him. One man is at the far right end of the catwalk beside a dark box or toolbox. None of them is tied off, none is holding a rail — the catwalk treads are open slats with the sea directly beneath. A loose rope hangs down from the platform into empty air. No safety net in frame. Blown-out white sky throughout, so the men read as near-silhouettes.
notes: The aspect ratio is the problem: 1034 x 400. It is close to a letterbox strip already and will not fill a 16:9 deck without heavy upscaling; best used as a banded or matted insert. Content-wise it is exactly the theme — a riveting-era gang out on the walkway with no fall protection.

attribution: Fred Lyon, 'Painting under the roadbed, Alcatraz in distance', 1950 — posted by SF Camerawork (auction lot, print donated by the artist and Peter Fetterman Gallery)
depicts: A black-and-white photograph taken from inside the steel underneath the Golden Gate Bridge roadway. A single man is silhouetted against the bright water, standing on a steeply raked diagonal girder, reaching both arms up to grip the structure above his head. Behind him a large square-mesh safety screen fills the whole opening between the steel members; the bay glares white beyond it, with a low dark island silhouette (Alcatraz) on the horizon. Heavy riveted trusses frame the top and left of the frame; a chain hangs down at centre and a coiled rope lies on the walkway at bottom right.
details: One man, in silhouette — no readable clothing detail, no visible hard hat outline, no harness or lanyard. He is standing on the sloping web of a girder with both hands overhead, which is how a painter moves along the underside. The mesh screen behind him is the key detail for this theme: it is the closest thing in the pool to the look of a net slung under the deck, seen from a worker's position inside the steel. High-contrast, almost graphic — near-black steel, blown-white water.
notes: This is Fred Lyon's well-known 1950 photograph, thirteen years after the bridge opened, so it is maintenance painting and not construction — say so if narration points at it. 840 x 872 is at the low end but above bar; a near-square crop, awkward for a 16:9 deck without a background fill. Non-commercial licence.

depicts: Modern colour photograph looking along the east edge of the Golden Gate Bridge deck from the sidewalk. A maintenance platform is cantilevered out over the water off the side of the deck, and a lone worker in a full white protective coverall and orange hard hat stands on it with his back to the camera. Cars are queued on the roadway at left, the orange suspender ropes and lamp standards march away into fog, and the grey-green water of the bay fills the right half of the frame with a small ferry wake far below. More workers in hard hats are visible further along the deck edge behind him.
details: One worker in the foreground plus roughly four more small figures on the deck further back. The near man wears a white disposable coverall with the hood up under an orange hard hat — full containment gear for lead-paint removal — and stands inside a mesh-sided platform with a proper handrail, which is exactly the protection the 1930s crews did not have. The platform is bolted to the outside of the girder and hangs clear of the deck over open water. Rivet heads run in rows across every steel surface. Alcatraz-side hills and a low fog bank close the background.
notes: The photographer's caption states the bridge employs 38 painters and 17 ironworkers — a usable present-day counterpoint to the Depression-era crew. Portrait orientation. Non-commercial licence. Directly rhymes with labor-safety-06 (same job, sixty years apart).

depicts: Looking straight up into the underbelly of the Golden Gate Bridge on the Marin side. The frame is filled with the coffered grid of the deck's underside — rectangular bays of weathered blue-green and rust-stained steel plate — crossed by a bright orange-red riveted truss and, running horizontally through the middle, a galvanised catwalk and handrail used by maintenance crews. Green spray-painted graffiti is scrawled on the plating at right.
details: No people. The graffiti at right, painted on the underside plating where only a worker could reach it, reads IRONWORKERS in tall green letters, with a partial tag above it. Everything else is structure: the plate bays show decades of paint failure and water staining, the orange truss and its gusset plates are freshly painted, and the catwalk is grated steel with a yellow-marked kickboard. The point of the frame is the signature, not the steel.
visible_text: Green spray-painted graffiti on the deck underside at right: 'IRONWORKERS'
notes: Exactly 800px on the long edge — at the size floor, fine full-frame, no crops. No-derivatives licence, so it must be used uncropped. A literal, present-tense claim of authorship by the trade, useful as a closing image for the labour thread.

depicts: Telephoto view down onto the Golden Gate Bridge deck from Battery Spencer, taken during the January 2015 installation of the moveable median barrier. Two orange Toyota forklifts and a white pickup are working in the closed traffic lanes, laying a line of white concrete-and-steel barrier segments down the centre of the roadway; a flatbed trailer stacked with more segments waits at bottom left. On the pedestrian sidewalk at upper left a crowd of cyclists and walkers, and two men in dark coats leaning on the rail, watch the work. Water fills the top left corner and the bridge's own suspender ropes and railings frame the shot.
details: About ten workers plus a dozen or more onlookers. Every worker is in high-visibility yellow-green — hi-vis vests or full jackets — and a hard hat (white on the forklift driver at centre, yellow on the two men guiding the barrier, yellow on the driver at left, more on the crew by the pickup at right). One man in a hi-vis jacket walks the centreline with a hand tool; another rides a small white utility cart at right. Traffic cones, blue layout marks painted on the asphalt, and a marked STATEWIDE TRAFFIC SAFETY pickup complete the scene. Modern, fully-regulated site discipline — the visual opposite of the 1930s frames in this pool.
visible_text: Small lettering on the white pickup door at right reads 'STATEWIDE / TRAFFIC SAFETY & SIGNS'. A taxi-style roof sign on the black car at centre.
notes: Present-day counterpoint image: hi-vis, hard hats, lane closures, spectators. No height work and no fall exposure — it is deck-level work.

depicts: Taken from the Golden Gate Bridge sidewalk looking north-west along the Pacific side of the deck. A fine steel mesh net runs the length of the bridge, slung out horizontally from below the sidewalk on regularly spaced orange outrigger arms, receding to a vanishing point. The water of the Pacific fills the right half of the frame with low sun glittering off it, the Marin Headlands run along the horizon, and cars and the orange pedestrian railing are visible at far left.
details: No people. The net is the subject: a continuous grey mesh apron about twenty feet wide hanging clear of the deck edge on painted orange brackets, each bracket picked out along the receding line, with a taut cable running along its outer edge. Foreground detail is a heavy riveted orange girder and a maintenance rail. This is the modern suicide-deterrent net, completed in the early 2020s — structurally and visually it is the same idea as the 1936 construction net slung under the deck, and it is the only free-licensed photograph found of any net hanging beneath this bridge.
visible_text: A small stencilled panel number, '48'-something, on the girder at top left.
notes: IMPORTANT: this is the 2018-2024 suicide-deterrent net, NOT the 1936 construction safety net. It is offered as a visual stand-in / rhyme only, and narration must not present it as the historical net. No photograph of the 1936 net at usable resolution was found — see report.

depicts: Studio close-up of a single original Golden Gate Bridge rivet lying on a plain white background, lit so it casts a soft shadow. The domed head at left is coated in bright orange-red bridge paint; the cylindrical shank runs to the right in bare blue-grey steel with visible shear marks and tool scoring, and the far end is split and peeled back into a ragged flange where it was cut out.
details: No people. The head is roughly one and a half times the diameter of the shank, matching the uploader's note that the shaft was 1 inch and the head 1.5 inches. Orange paint covers only the head — the part that was exposed to weather — while the shank stayed bare inside the steel. The mushroomed, torn end shows it was burned or sheared out rather than drilled. Shot large in frame, so it works as a full-screen object.
notes: Direct visual for the rivet counts — roughly 600,000 rivets per tower, well over a million in the bridge. The uploader states original rivets were removed and replaced with high-strength bolts during later retrofits, which is where surviving specimens like this came from. Near-duplicate subject to labor-safety-12, but a different rivet, different photographer and a different condition (this one sheared and brightly painted).

depicts: Studio close-up of an original 1930s Golden Gate Bridge rivet lying on a white surface, head to the right, shank to the left. The domed head is patchy orange-red where the original bridge paint survives, worn through to black scale and bare grey metal in places; the shank is dark corroded steel with a rough sheared end.
details: No people. Compared with labor-safety-11 this rivet reads as older and more weathered — the paint is broken up into islands, the steel is pitted, and the head-to-shank transition shows a burr where it was cut. Photographed smaller in the frame with more white space around it, so it holds up as a slower, quieter object shot.
notes: Photographer's note: the original rivets were removed and replaced with stronger bolts during 1970s-80s retrofit work, which is how originals entered private hands. Same subject as labor-safety-11; keep both only if two different rivet beats are wanted, otherwise 11 is higher resolution and more permissively licensed. Non-commercial licence.

attribution: Carol M. Highsmith — Jon B. Lovelace Collection of California Photographs, Library of Congress
depicts: A full-length bronze statue of Joseph Baermann Strauss standing on a low circular concrete plinth in a paved plaza at the bridge's south approach. He is in a three-piece suit, hands at his sides, holding a rolled document in his left hand. Behind him are flowering coastal plantings — yellow bush daisies, purple echium spikes — a retaining wall with an interpretive banner, and, catching the sun at upper right, the top of the Golden Gate Bridge's south tower against a cloudless blue sky. Two or three small figures are on the walkway at left.
details: The bronze is weathered to a green-brown patina. A small dedication plaque is set into the plinth at his feet. The white band around the plinth's rim carries the '75th anniversary' fundraising legend and sponsor names. Sharp, high-resolution and evenly lit — a clean, unfussy portrait of the man who insisted on the $130,000 net over the objections that it was exorbitant.
visible_text: Around the plinth rim: 'JOSEPH STRAUSS LEGACY CIRCLE — Take your place in the Strauss Circle and support the Golden Gate Bridge's legacy for generations to come. www.goldengatebridge75.org'. Sponsor names at left include Odwalla, Chevron, Hanson Bridgett LLP, Levi Strauss & Co., Pacific Gas and Electric Company, Speck Products; at right 'STRAUSS CIRCLE LEAD GIFT', 'Lisa and Douglas Goldman Fund', 'Bank of America'. Small plaque on the statue base reads '1870 JOSEPH B. STRAUSS 1938'.
notes: Public domain, very high resolution, portrait orientation. Included here because the safety net and the hard-hat / tie-off / goggles rules were all Strauss's mandates; the Strauss design story itself may belong to another theme. The modern sponsor lettering on the plinth is prominent and will read on screen — crop it out if that is unwanted.

depicts: Modern colour photograph, shot on a long lens from below against a plain blue sky: two ironworkers perched on a bare steel frame during erection. The man on the left, in a brown hard hat and sunglasses, straddles a beam and reaches up with a gloved hand to steady a vertical column; the man on the right, in a red hard hat and white T-shirt, is bent over the beam with a spud wrench, tool belt and leather nail bag hanging off his harness. A rigging cable with a hook runs down between them; a third worker's gloved hand and forearm intrude at the right edge.
details: Two and a half men. Both wear hard hats — one brown with union stickers, one red — and both wear full-body fall-arrest harnesses with yellow shoulder straps clearly visible over the shoulders and around the thighs, though neither lanyard is shown clipped to anything in frame. Both wear heavy tan boots and gloves. Chalk erection marks are scrawled across the girders ('SOUTH', 'CJM', bay numbers). Beam bolt holes, a shackle and a red pin visible. Sharp, high-contrast, blue sky behind — reads instantly as 'ironworkers on high steel'.
visible_text: Chalk-marked on the steel: 'SOUTH', 'CJM', and various erection numbers such as '08.09' and bay marks.
notes: NOT the Golden Gate Bridge and not historic — this is the steel frame of a new building at Massachusetts General Hospital, 2006, sourced from the Wikipedia 'Ironworker' article as generic trade B-roll. Use only where the narration is about the trade rather than about this bridge, and do not imply otherwise. Included because it is the only high-resolution, permissively licensed image in the pool that shows ironworkers' faces, harnesses and hard hats up close.

depicts: A bronze memorial statue of an ironworker outside a union hall. The figure stands on a rusted steel I-beam that is cantilevered off a short concrete pier, one arm thrown straight up above his head in a signal, the other holding his hard hat against his chest. He wears a work shirt, belted trousers with a spud wrench and bull pin hanging from the belt, and heavy boots. Behind him is a grey concrete-block building wall with ivy on a wrought-iron trellis, glass entrance doors and a partly visible street number; an A-frame sign stands at right.
details: One figure, a statue, not a live worker. The detail that matters for this theme is the hard hat held in his hands rather than worn — the memorial convention for the dead — and the raised hand, the ironworker's signal to a crane. The I-beam he stands on is genuine weathering steel, mounted at head height, so the statue is literally standing on high steel over a paved forecourt. Blue sky with broken cloud behind.
visible_text: Building number partly visible at right: '851…'. The A-frame sign's text is illegible at this resolution.
notes: NOT at the Golden Gate Bridge — this is at an Iron Workers Local 535 hall (BSOIW). Offered as a memorial / union-labour image for the eleven dead or for the 'proud union ironworkers built it' beat. Portrait orientation, high resolution. Say clearly in narration that it is a union memorial elsewhere, not a Golden Gate monument.
